message.content:
The total number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large—on the order of **\(10^{43}\)**.  

This figure comes from counting all ways the 32 pieces (16 per side) can be arranged on the 64 squares while respecting the rules of chess (e.g., no two kings in check, pawns only on ranks 2–7, etc.).  It’s often cited as “the Shannon number” (≈ 10^120) when referring to the total number of possible games (sequences of moves), but the number of *positions* themselves is roughly \(10^{43}\).
